title: make an offering, weave your web
content:
from my podcast: botanical studies of internet magic
listen on spotify / listen on apple

when tending to my business, I bring it back to two practices -- making offerings, and weaving my web. I share how I think about offerings as sacred containers, organic shapes, and potent distillations of your creative energy -- into usable form.

I'll talk about weaving your web as an energetically efficient, long-term strategy that builds your body of work, and invites people into your world. this episode is about all perspective shifts -- to reimagining business as a generative, potent creative practice.

This is part two of our mini series. In the last episode, I talked about the foundation for a public creative practice, make the work, share the work. Today, we'll talk about building a business ecosystem that can support and sustain your life, exploring what an offering really is as a way of distilling and channeling creative energy into usable form. We'll talk about what an ecosystem web is made out of and why I prefer to think about weaving a web instead of launching an offering. And I will share some concrete examples from my own business and creative practice.

If you'd like to work together on the step-by-step process, the how, I'm teaching a live course starting in early March called Digital Abundance and it'll be self-paced afterwards.

how do I get paid?

Let's start by talking about the central problem that I often hear and that I've also experienced, which is I'm tired of making and sharing work for free. How do I share work that I can get paid for? How do I receive money or value for my work? How do I build a business that can sustain me?

The first thing that I'll say to preface my answers to all of these questions is that building a business is about creating a system or structure that generates energy and nourishment for you and for those that you serve. It's not a set and forget kind of thing. It is literally about weaving a web, thread by thread, offering by offering and letting it be flexible and adaptable to you, to where you are in the current season of your life.

It reminds me of a post that I wrote last year called, "My business is a hammock I weave by hand," which is to say making a business takes time, deep attention and patience, not just to find something that works for other people, but something that really aligns with who you are and how you want to work.

So I'll remind you of the guiding principles I shared from the previous episode, that whatever you make or share or build, I believe these four things are really important. Number one, feeling a sense of agency and autonomy in your work. Number two, finding pleasure in the process. Number three, that the whole thing is generative and regenerative, it creates more energy the more that you do it. And number four, that it feels authentic and true to who you are, which is always changing of course.

unpacking the core problem

What I notice as the core problem is that we often feel free and spontaneous when making things for ourselves, but when we're called to make things for other people, when we're being paid to make something for clients or for students or customers, it can create this vacuum of pressure. It makes us feel like we're being put into a cage or we're losing a sense of freedom. Maybe it makes us feel like we have to perform to contort ourselves to do some sales and marketing acrobatics to prove our worthiness that if you're gonna give me money, suddenly the stakes feel high, suddenly it no longer feels as fun to do what we're doing before.

It makes me think of like stage fright. Maybe you can sing in the shower, but the moment you get on stage, your vocal cords just freeze up.

To use that metaphor, I think the secret here is to always sing for others, create paid offerings as if you're singing in the shower alone, bringing your artistic energy, your true voice, your desire to everything that you do, whether it's paid or unpaid, letting there be no difference, which is so hard, I recognize that.

I think this requires a deep self-trust, a confidence in what you have as being worthy of value, whether that value is attention or time or money. Self-confidence is a muscle that you build over time. It can feel like audacity at first, like how dare I charge money for this. Doing this work requires that you have a capacity to feel like a failure, to feel not enough, to feel shame and embarrassment, and to have the resilience to get up from that place.

Over time, what I found that it's embodying two sides of the same coin to trust that when you're writing a post for your website or making art, while it's not directly making you money per se, it is building the web of your ecosystem, which leads people into your world. And as you're making an offering, a paid offering, do it with the same freedom and play and spontaneity with which you make creative work that's just for you. That is to bring your artist energy to everything that you do and to trust that electricity as what animates who you are and what you have to give to the world.

This is really a journey of decompartmentalization, which I wrote about a couple of years ago in a post called "The Way of the Artist Entrepreneur."

make an offering

What does it mean to make an offering? Well, we've talked about the word make in episode one, how the energy of making applies to everything that you do, whether it's making your art, making a podcast, making a newsletter or a paid course or service.

So what is an offering? I want to talk about how I think of offerings as sacred gifts. My interpretation of offerings within the business structure of products, services, subscriptions, and how I think of offerings as distilled magnetic containers for your energy.

offerings as sacred

I love the word offering because I think about leaving an offering at the altar. You leave it and walk away. There's a sacredness to it. I feel a sense of non-attachment to what happens. I don't need to refresh my phone and see who received my offering. I'm fully in the act of surrender.

So a personal story example. Last month, I was taking a walk through Prospect Park in Brooklyn with a friend, and it was a very difficult period of time for me. We sat down on a bench and discovered that there were three pieces of bead jewelry laid out in an arrangement, like it was left there for us to take. It felt like a gift from life.

This offering was free, but honestly, it felt like it had more value to me than something I choose to buy in a store for $20. It was something that I received, which felt sacred and priceless, which is to say that in your business and creative ecosystem, you can have offerings that are like gifts. I think of art as very much a sacred offering where the monetary value you attach to it is so much more elastic and fluid.

Whenever I get caught up in the business pressures of making an offering, I try to center myself in this spiritual foundation first, which is really about connecting to a felt sense of abundance. Whether or not this offering sells the amount that I wanted to sell, I can trust that I am safe. I can focus on creating and releasing my offering and release control to the outcomes.

offerings as business structures

Now let's move to the material interpretation of business offerings. So the general way that I think we're taught is that there's three types of offerings, products in which you make something, your customer pays once, and then they get the thing, services in which they engage in a relationship and process with you to get a desired outcome, and subscriptions like memberships or sub-stacks or communities in which they pay a monthly or annual fee. Then there's some combination of hybrid models between these three core types.

This is the typical definition, but I want you to think of these three categories as basic forms like circles or squares or triangles. You can round out the edges, you can make them more nuanced, you can think about your own way of relating to them. Which form of this offering is the best shape for me to distill, contain, and share my energy?

So I'll share some examples. I teach a wide range of courses. Technically, they're considered products. I do a live session once and then offer them as self-paced journeys, but I make it very clear that my courses are adventures. They are guided processes.

I also offer one-on-one services in which I'm guiding and facilitating a collaborative process. The outcome is never guaranteed, but there's a direct relationship and intimacy of being deep in the process with someone else, which is a specific way of relating to a service. Your work is building a collaborative relationship and there are infinite ways in which you can do that.

I also have a community offering, labyrinth, but while most communities tend to be monthly or annual, I've decided that mine should be seasonal. I relate to it as taking care of a community garden, creating a space and environment for my members, gathering an infinite feast for them.

And the last category is objects, which could be a book that I sell or a planner or a deck of tarot cards. Any distillation in object form, it's like I put my energy into this thing that you can access and be a part of without me. A zine could be an object, a postcard could be an object. I just prefer the word objects over products because it feels a little bit more like art, a bit more artful for me.

When I think about these different object shapes and forms, the way that I choose the right shape and adapt it to my specific offering is to think about the topic or theme. What's the best form to hold it? Does it want to be an object like a zine? Does it want to be an ongoing one-on-one collaboration like a service? Does it want to be a course?

I ask myself how much energy or what kind of energy do I want to spend to create this offering? And then once I've created it, how much ongoing energy do I want to keep pouring into it? How present do I want to be when other people are engaging with this offering?

offerings as distillation

I like to think about offerings as a distillation, extreme concentration of your creative energy that is magnetic, that draws people to the deepest layers of your world.

In other words, an offering is not something in raw form. I would not teach a course about quilt making because I've never made a quilt. I wouldn't teach a course about piano practice skills because even though they work for me, I don't think my knowledge has matured or ripened enough.

An offering is something that's gone through entire life cycles of metabolizing, which is not to say that this offering won't change. I truly believe that an offering should be alive. And this is also not to say that you can't make an offering about something you're just discovering. You could invite other people to be in the process of discovery with you. But I think in that case, the form of the offering should reflect that. It might be an offering that feels lighter or lower pressure or lower priced, not because you're not worthy of being paid for it, but because it takes off the pressure. It makes it feel more experimental and more exploratory. Again, this is not a hard rule of thumb. It's just one way of thinking about this.

Right now, most of my business ecosystem is built up of creative courses and they represent a distillation of a decade's worth of my work and process. When I feel ready to teach a course, it's like feeling ready to give birth because I can feel that energy wanting to consolidate and to be integrated at another dimension through me, through expression and sharing.

So when I imagine the form of an offering, I see it as this shining energy crystal that has magnetic powers. It's like everything you've lived and figured out and worked through existed as particles in the atmosphere. And the moment you create an offering, it magnetizes those particles into this dense energy form, which acts as a container for your own process and perspective. It forces you to articulate that and make it usable for others.

It's magnetic in that all of your work is swirling, organizing around that core offering. It's a consolidation of your emotional, creative, mental resources, and it receives other people's attention, investment, money, time. In that sense, an offering is like an open node, attracting value and giving value, consolidating your abundance and receiving abundance.

My question for you is what in your ecosystem, in your creative world, do you feel is ready to move through this alchemical process of synthesis, metabolizing, condensation, and distillation? What feels ready to create as an offering? What offering makes you feel like you are growing in the way that you want to grow? That can take you to the next level.

That's usually how I think about making offerings. I make the offering that I need to unlock the next level of my practice. Oftentimes it's things that I've been digesting, thinking, turning over in my head again and again for a very long time, and I need a little bit of a push, a little bit of external pressure, honestly, to make an explosion, a creative explosion out of it, which is turning all of that raw energy into frameworks, practices, processes, tools, resources that other people can use.

Another metaphor example that I like to use to describe offerings is that you can think about your public ecosystem website as like open gardens, public gardens, and then you can think of your offerings as private tinctures or herbal tonics that were made in your apothecary from specially grown medicinal plants. Offerings have been distilled to its most potent form that it can be quickly metabolized and absorbed in the bloodstream, but the raw source of those offerings already exist in your public gardens or your ecosystem web.

weave the web

Let's talk about what it means to weave the web.

Your web is your public body of work that builds threads of connection with anyone who arrives into your world. It can exist in any medium, in any form. Generally speaking, I think of the website as the container to hold your web. Your website is the world, which holds your podcasts, your writings, your art, and directs people to your newsletter.

So the practice of weaving the web is like the ongoing practice of gardening, taking care of your public gardens, allowing people to discover new things, new paths, and enjoy the abundance that you've created.

My entire philosophy and approach is built on a nonlinear integrated model of creativity and business. So in this web, everything is interconnected. Each of your offerings is like a node that is connected by threads to things that you've been talking about, writing about for years. It's like a spider web or a mycelium network or like a tree canopy.

When something lands on a spider web, the spider can feel it from anywhere. The threads are living and connected.

The purpose of your web is to allow discovery, allow people to wander through your web, like a garden, like a labyrinth, to enjoy themselves in your world without asking anything from them. It's this process of being in your web that you build trust and intimacy and abundance. Your web becomes something that is organically growing, alive, responsive.

distilled vs exploratory

I think of weaving the web as a separate practice from making the offering because an offering is the potent distillation, focusing of energy, whereas weaving the web is something that is more diffuse, free, exploratory, tangential.

The purpose of your web or your world, those words are interchangeable, is not to sell anything. It's to guide people along their own choose your adventure journey of discovery, offering them your creative abundance, infinite pathways of exploring your work.

I write about the distinction between wandering through a web versus forcing someone to fall down a marketing funnel. In this post, build a labyrinth, not a marketing funnel, which mostly argues that agency and autonomy for your visitors is a far better long-term strategy to building a financially sustainable business than using marketing or sales tactics that attempt to override people's objections and pull them down through sheer gravity to buy something.

All this is say it's really important to design and weave your web in a way that feels aligned with your creative process. The process must feel pleasurable to you. It must feel regenerative. Every day could be one tiny new thread, but over a period of months or years, you can zoom out and see the shimmering, beautiful structure of your web as your world.

web weaving vs launching

I want to make the distinction between weaving a web versus the typical launch strategy.

Personally, I don't love the word launch because it feels very much like a short-term effort. The word launch feels kind of phallic also, and there's a lot of urgency-based sales and marketing in the launch strategy. Maybe you're supposed to send emails, have a whole nurturing sequence, dangle some carrots and discounts and try to push them over the edge.

This just feels very tiring, and knowing myself, I can't do anything that feels tiring. So weaving a web is my approach to quote-unquote sales and marketing that is generative. I think about it more as like making a womb or a cocoon.

My general rule of thumb is that I make things for my web that don't become irrelevant once the launch window ends. So when I write emails, they can't just be sales emails. My guiding questions for myself are, will this thing that I'm making or doing still serve my ecosystem in one to two years' time? Will this thing that I'm sharing serve people who don't want this particular offering but are connected with my work in other ways?

Launching and offering feels hyper goal-oriented to convert, to have more sales, but weaving a web is more focused on building relationships. It's allowing people to have different entry points, different ways of relating to my work. It's less urgent, which is not to say that there's no focus containers.

I do think you need containers like deadlines and dates and registration windows in order to focus the experience for yourself more than anything. The reason why I offer my courses as live sessions is so that I can be in the collaborative process of making the course with a group of people in a contained window of time. But that's very different than using urgency as a marketing or manipulation tactic. The containers serve an energetic purpose beyond selling something.

concrete example of weaving a web

Let me give you a concrete example of how this might work. I am currently releasing a new offering called Money Juice Cleanse, which will exist as a live session and then as a self-paced course.

So step one for weaving the web is to notice what already exists. I look through my archives and think about what have I written about money and I organize it. I connect the threads of the existing web.

Step two is to create a little tasting menu, like a preview, a free offering that can show a taster of what's behind the paid container, maybe I'll record a podcast episode or make a zine about it.

Then step three is to nurture the web as an ongoing practice. This might happen after my launch window in which I keep making art or illustrations or writings around money topics. And each time I make something that is related to this topic, I add it to my body of work, my curated page of money-related writings, and then I offer people a pathway, like leaving a breadcrumb trail. If you want more distilled guidance, you can explore my course, Money Juice Cleanse.

Then step four is that once I make other offerings that are related to this offering, I connect the nodes in a constellation. So for example, Money Juice Cleanse is a warmup to my business course, Digital Abundance. And then maybe I'll create pathways between those two different mini ecosystems and let them cross-pollinate.

two purposes of weaving

I give you this example to show you that there are two purposes of weaving a web.

For me, it's an ongoing creative practice, very queens of wands energy, which allows me to deepen my work. It's a way of mastery. As I weave the web, I refine my understanding, I discover new concepts. It's an inner process of alchemy that prepares me for the intensive sprint that is creating an offering.

And for the visitors of my world, it offers many pathways, it offers a journey of discovery for them to explore.

the web redistributes pressure

When I think about the system or structure of a web, I think about how one of its primary features is that it redistributes pressure or weight. What I mean by that is, people can travel around your entire web, your entire world, they can devour everything you've created, and maybe they never buy anything from you. And that's totally fine, because there will be a portion of people who do want to engage deeper, who do want to be a part of your paid offerings. And you have to trust that that number of people will be enough to keep the entire system feeling regenerative.

Perhaps the people who only absorb your public gardens, perhaps they will pollinate your world in other ways. Buying something is just one way of relating to your body of work. And I know this requires so much trust that if you give your abundance, you will receive abundance.

This strategy is not about trying to optimize sales on one thing, but about tending to the entire ecosystem, seeing how everything is connected, your creativity, your artist energy with your paid offerings, seeing what your entire world needs in order to be abundant and to thrive.

closing notes

So when you wake up in the morning and you're not sure what to do with your creative life, my minimalist instructions are, make the work, share the work. When you wake up in the morning and you're not sure what to do with your business, make an offering, weave your web. Trust that each thread you weave of your web will be a channel for your creative abundance and that this channel goes both ways.

And so I wanna close with three simple questions for you to think about. What offerings or topics feel ready to be distilled right now? What ecosystem web already exists in your body of work? And what do you feel inspired to continue weaving in your web?

In the next episode, we'll talk about how to make art the center of your world, the life force that flows through your web and through your offerings.

~

Take care, speak soon.
